title: Emotions and Moods
description: Precise words for how people feel, from quiet contentment to intense joy.

cards.meaning: Having or showing a gentle, slightly sad longing, often for something in the past.
examples: She gave a wistful smile as she looked through her old photographs.

cards.meaning: Extremely happy and excited, usually because of something good that has happened.
examples: The team was elated when the proposal was approved.

cards.meaning: A deep, quiet sadness that lasts, often without an obvious cause.
examples: A soft melancholy settled over the town once the festival had ended.

cards.meaning: Easily annoyed or made angry.
examples: Lack of sleep made him irritable all morning.

cards.meaning: Quietly satisfied and at peace with what you have.
examples: She was content with a simple life and a good book.

cards.meaning: Worried or nervous that something bad may happen.
examples: Many staff were apprehensive about the restructuring.

cards.meaning: Nervous and unable to relax.
examples: Everyone was on edge while we waited for the results.

cards.meaning: Extremely pleased and happy.
examples: My parents were over the moon when I passed my exams.

cards.meaning: Feeling sad and lacking energy.
examples: He has been in low spirits since his best friend moved away.

cards.meaning: Feeling intense happiness and excitement, often for a short time.
examples: The crowd was euphoric after the final whistle.

title: Workplace Communication
description: Everyday phrases for meetings, emails and teamwork in a professional setting.

cards.meaning: To make brief contact with someone to share an update.
examples: Let's touch base on Friday to review our progress.

cards.meaning: To take further action after an earlier contact or meeting.
examples: I will follow up with the client after the meeting.

cards.meaning: To include someone in a conversation or email thread so they stay informed.
examples: Please loop me in on any emails about the budget.

cards.meaning: Sharing the same understanding of a situation or plan.
examples: Before we start, let's make sure we are all on the same page.

cards.meaning: The time or energy a person has available to take on work.
examples: I'm afraid I don't have the bandwidth to lead another project this month.

cards.meaning: To return to a topic later.
examples: We can circle back to the pricing question next week.

cards.meaning: A specific task agreed during a meeting, usually with an owner and a deadline.
examples: Each action item should have a clear owner and due date.

cards.meaning: A person or group with an interest in, or affected by, an organisation or project.
examples: We interviewed key stakeholders before drafting the communication plan.

cards.meaning: Open and honest, with nothing important hidden.
examples: Management tried to be transparent about the reasons for the change.

cards.meaning: Brief but clear and complete.
examples: Keep your update concise; the director only has five minutes.

title: Academic Writing
description: Formal vocabulary that helps you argue, evaluate and support claims in essays and reports.

cards.meaning: To provide evidence that supports a claim.
examples: You need to substantiate this claim with recent data.

cards.meaning: To combine ideas from different sources into a single, coherent whole. (American spelling: synthesize)
examples: A strong literature review synthesises findings rather than listing them.

cards.meaning: Logical, well organised and easy to follow.
examples: Each paragraph should build a coherent argument.

cards.meaning: To use cautious language so that a claim is not stated too strongly.
examples: Researchers often hedge their conclusions with words such as 'may' and 'suggest'.

cards.meaning: Based on observation, experiment or experience rather than theory alone.
examples: The study provides empirical evidence for the effect.

cards.meaning: Considering or because of (new information).
examples: In light of these findings, the policy should be reviewed.

cards.meaning: Mostly; in many ways but not completely.
examples: The audit was, to a large extent, successful.

cards.meaning: Despite; without being prevented by.
examples: Notwithstanding its limitations, the study offers useful insights.

cards.meaning: An idea or statement that an argument is based on.
examples: The argument rests on the premise that staff read every memo.

cards.meaning: A detailed analysis and judgement of a work or idea; to give such an analysis.
examples: Write a critique of the survey design, noting its strengths and weaknesses.

title: The Art of Persuasion
description: Language for convincing others, building arguments and winning people over.

cards.meaning: So convincing or interesting that it holds your attention.
examples: She made a compelling case for flexible working hours.

cards.meaning: The art of persuasive speaking or writing; sometimes used negatively for language that sounds impressive but lacks substance.
examples: The speech relied more on rhetoric than on evidence.

cards.meaning: To persuade someone to support you or agree with you.
examples: Her honesty won over the sceptical audience.

cards.meaning: To try to persuade by focusing on a particular feeling, value or reason.
examples: The advertisement appeals to parents' desire to keep their children safe.

cards.meaning: To influence someone's opinion or decision.
examples: Personal stories can sway an audience more than statistics.

cards.meaning: An argument that opposes another argument.
examples: Address the strongest counterargument before you conclude.

cards.meaning: To admit, often reluctantly, that something is true.
examples: He conceded that the costs were higher than expected.

cards.meaning: To give reasons in support of something.
examples: The report makes a case for investing in staff training.

cards.meaning: Clear, logical and convincing.
examples: She presented a cogent argument for reform.

cards.meaning: To persuade someone to change their mind.
examples: It took an hour, but we finally talked him round.

title: Nature and the Seasons
description: Descriptive words for landscapes, plants and the turning of the year.

cards.meaning: Green with grass or growing plants.
examples: We drove through verdant hills covered in tea plantations.

cards.meaning: Marked with patches of light and shade, or spots of colour.
examples: We walked along a path dappled with sunlight.

cards.meaning: The leaves of a plant or tree, considered together.
examples: The autumn foliage turned the valley red and gold.

cards.meaning: To produce flowers; a flower or the state of flowering.
examples: The cherry trees bloom for only a few weeks each spring.

cards.meaning: To become dry, weak and shrunken.
examples: Without water, the plants began to wither.

cards.meaning: The day with the longest or shortest period of daylight in the year.
examples: The June solstice is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

cards.meaning: Alive but temporarily inactive or not growing.
examples: Many trees remain dormant through the winter.

cards.meaning: Growing thickly, richly and healthily.
examples: The garden was lush after weeks of rain.

cards.meaning: One of the two times each year when day and night are roughly equal in length.
examples: At the equinox, day and night are roughly equal everywhere on Earth.

cards.meaning: Something new and refreshing that improves a situation.
examples: Her ideas were a breath of fresh air in a dull meeting.

title: Cities and Travel
description: Words and phrases for exploring places, planning journeys and describing cities.

cards.meaning: Full of busy, energetic activity.
examples: We explored a bustling night market in the old town.

cards.meaning: Far from popular or well-known places.
examples: They stayed in a quiet village off the beaten track.

cards.meaning: A planned route or schedule for a journey.
examples: Our itinerary includes three days in Melaka.

cards.meaning: A strong desire to travel.
examples: Her wanderlust took her across six continents.

cards.meaning: A short stop between parts of a journey, especially between flights.
examples: We had a four-hour layover in Doha.

cards.meaning: Including people and influences from many different countries and cultures.
examples: Kuala Lumpur is a cosmopolitan city with food from around the world.

cards.meaning: To begin a journey.
examples: We set off before sunrise to avoid the traffic.

cards.meaning: The uncontrolled spread of a city into the surrounding countryside.
examples: Urban sprawl has replaced much of the old farmland.

cards.meaning: A building or place that is easy to recognise and helps people know where they are.
examples: The twin towers are the city's most famous landmark.

cards.meaning: To travel from place to place.
examples: It is easy to get around the city by train.

title: Time and Patience
description: Expressions about timing, waiting and the passing of time.

cards.meaning: Just before it is too late.
examples: We submitted the report in the nick of time.

cards.meaning: Lasting for a very short time.
examples: We caught a fleeting glimpse of the eagle before it vanished.

cards.meaning: Lasting a very short time; more formal or poetic than 'brief'.
examples: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.

cards.meaning: To wait patiently for the right moment to act.
examples: She bided her time until a senior position became available.

cards.meaning: Lasting longer than expected or usual.
examples: The negotiations were protracted and exhausting.

cards.meaning: At the appropriate time; eventually.
examples: You will receive your results in due course.

cards.meaning: Continued effort to achieve something despite difficulty or delay.
examples: Learning a language well requires perseverance.

cards.meaning: Time seems to pass very quickly.
examples: Time flies when you enjoy your work.

cards.meaning: To wait for a short time; or to keep going in a difficult situation.
examples: Hold on, I'll check the schedule.

cards.meaning: The period between two events; temporary, for that period.
examples: In the interim, Sarah will manage the team.

title: Money and Value
description: Vocabulary for spending, saving and judging what something is worth.

cards.meaning: Careful with money and avoiding waste.
examples: Living frugally helped her save for a master's degree.

cards.meaning: Spending much more than is necessary or sensible.
examples: The launch party was extravagant for a small start-up.

cards.meaning: To have just enough money to pay for what you need.
examples: Many families struggle to make ends meet.

cards.meaning: Something that costs far more than it is worth.
examples: Twenty ringgit for a bottle of water is a rip-off.

cards.meaning: Wealthy; having plenty of money.
examples: They grew up in an affluent neighbourhood.

cards.meaning: Extremely useful. Note: it does not mean 'without value'.
examples: Her advice was invaluable during my first year at university.

cards.meaning: To spend a lot of money on something enjoyable.
examples: We splashed out on a nice dinner to celebrate.

cards.term: cost an arm and a leg
cards.meaning: To be very expensive.
examples: That new laptop cost an arm and a leg.

cards.meaning: To plan how you will spend money; a plan of income and spending.
examples: Students should budget carefully for the semester.

cards.meaning: Worth the time, money or effort spent.
examples: The extra training proved worthwhile.

title: Conflict and Resolution
description: Words for disagreements and the ways people settle them.

cards.meaning: A strained feeling between people or groups that may lead to conflict.
examples: There was tension between the two departments.

cards.meaning: To remove misunderstanding or bad feeling by talking openly.
examples: A frank conversation helped to clear the air.

cards.meaning: An agreement in which each side gives up something it wanted.
examples: After hours of discussion, they reached a compromise.

cards.meaning: To become more serious or intense.
examples: The disagreement escalated into a formal complaint.

cards.meaning: To help two opposing sides reach an agreement.
examples: HR was asked to mediate between the manager and her team.

cards.meaning: To end a quarrel and become friendly again.
examples: After years of rivalry, the two writers buried the hatchet.

cards.meaning: A complaint about being treated unfairly.
examples: Staff can raise a grievance through the official process.

cards.meaning: In disagreement or conflict.
examples: The two reports are at odds over the cause of the decline.

cards.meaning: To restore friendly relations; or to make two ideas fit together.
examples: They reconciled after a long silence.

cards.meaning: Opinions or interests shared by people who otherwise disagree.
examples: Despite their differences, they found common ground on safety.

title: Memory and Nostalgia
description: Language for remembering, forgetting and longing for the past.

cards.meaning: A sentimental longing for a happy time in the past.
examples: The old song filled her with nostalgia.

cards.meaning: To talk or think with pleasure about past experiences.
examples: We spent the evening reminiscing about our school days.

cards.meaning: Very clear, detailed and bright in the mind.
examples: I have a vivid memory of my first day at university.

cards.meaning: Unclear or vague.
examples: My memories of that trip are hazy.

cards.meaning: To sound familiar.
examples: The name rings a bell, but I can't remember where we met.

cards.term: on the tip of my tongue
cards.meaning: Almost remembered but not quite.
examples: His name is on the tip of my tongue.

cards.meaning: To honour and remember an important person or event.
examples: A plaque commemorates the founders of the school.

cards.meaning: Bringing strong images, memories or feelings to mind.
examples: The writer's descriptions of the coast are wonderfully evocative.

cards.meaning: To help someone remember something.
examples: Looking at the photos might jog your memory.

cards.meaning: Belonging to an earlier time.
examples: The film captures the charm of a bygone era.

title: Art and Creativity
description: Words for making things, finding inspiration and judging creative work.

cards.meaning: A person or thing that inspires an artist or writer.
examples: The sea was her muse for many years.

cards.meaning: A set of ideas about beauty or style; relating to beauty and appearance.
examples: The app has a clean, minimalist aesthetic.

cards.meaning: Placing two different things side by side to highlight the contrast between them.
examples: The juxtaposition of old and new buildings is striking.

cards.meaning: New, experimental and ahead of its time, especially in the arts.
examples: The gallery shows avant-garde work by young artists.

cards.meaning: To think creatively and in an original way.
examples: We need to think outside the box to solve this problem.

cards.meaning: An outstanding work of art; a person's best work.
examples: Many critics consider the novel her masterpiece.

cards.meaning: To create or perform something without preparation.
examples: When the slides failed, she improvised brilliantly.

cards.meaning: Copying the ideas of others too closely; not original.
examples: Critics found the album derivative and predictable.

cards.meaning: A natural talent for something; stylishness.
examples: He has a flair for graphic design.

cards.term: in the eye of the beholder
cards.meaning: From 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder': beauty is a matter of personal opinion.
examples: Whether the building is beautiful is in the eye of the beholder.

title: Food and Flavour
description: Descriptive words for taste, texture and the pleasure of eating.

cards.meaning: Salty or spicy rather than sweet. (American spelling: savory)
examples: I prefer savoury snacks to sweets.

cards.meaning: Having a sharp, pleasantly sour taste.
examples: The tangy tamarind sauce balanced the rich fish.

cards.meaning: Having a strong, pleasant smell.
examples: The curry was rich with aromatic spices such as star anise and cinnamon.

cards.meaning: Lacking strong flavour; dull.
examples: The soup was bland, so I added some chilli.

cards.meaning: Juicy and tender in a pleasant way.
examples: The grilled chicken was succulent and perfectly seasoned.

cards.meaning: A person's sense of taste.
examples: The tasting menu was designed to delight the palate.

cards.meaning: To make you want more of something.
examples: The trailer whetted my appetite for the film.

cards.meaning: Something very easy to do.
examples: The first quiz was a piece of cake.

cards.meaning: Good for your health; also morally good.
examples: She cooks simple, wholesome meals for her family.

cards.meaning: So tasty that you want to keep eating more.
examples: These crackers are dangerously moreish.

title: Technology and the Digital World
description: Vocabulary for devices, software and life online.

cards.meaning: No longer used because something newer has replaced it.
examples: Fax machines are almost obsolete in most offices.

cards.meaning: The newest and most advanced.
examples: The lab uses cutting-edge equipment.

cards.meaning: Easy for people to use or understand.
examples: The new portal is far more user-friendly than the old one.

cards.meaning: A small, sudden fault in a system or machine.
examples: A glitch in the system delayed payments for a day.

cards.meaning: To make a process simpler and more efficient.
examples: The software streamlines the approval process.

cards.meaning: To make a copy of data so it is not lost.
examples: Always back up your work before installing an update.

cards.meaning: The record of data a person leaves behind through their online activity.
examples: Be careful what you post; your digital footprint can last for years.

cards.meaning: To find and fix problems in a system.
examples: The IT team spent the morning troubleshooting the network.

cards.meaning: Easy to understand and use without instructions.
examples: The interface is so intuitive that no training is needed.

cards.meaning: To spread very quickly and widely online.
examples: Her video went viral overnight.

title: Health and Wellbeing
description: Words for looking after the body and mind.

cards.meaning: Physical and emotional exhaustion caused by long-term stress.
examples: Long hours led to burnout among the nurses.

cards.meaning: Involving a lot of sitting and little physical activity.
examples: A sedentary lifestyle increases several health risks.

cards.meaning: To recover from illness, injury or tiredness.
examples: He took a week off to recuperate after surgery.

cards.meaning: Treating the whole person or system, not just one part.
examples: The clinic takes a holistic approach to patient care.

cards.meaning: Slightly ill.
examples: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.

cards.meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulties.
examples: Children are often more resilient than adults expect.

cards.meaning: To relax after a period of work or stress.
examples: I unwind by walking in the park after work.

cards.meaning: In very good health.
examples: My grandfather is eighty and still fit as a fiddle.

cards.meaning: The habit of avoiding excess.
examples: Sweets are fine in moderation.

cards.meaning: Consciously aware of something; attentive to the present moment.
examples: Try to be mindful of your posture when you work at a desk.

title: Friendship and Loyalty
description: Language for close bonds, trust and the people who stand by us.

cards.meaning: A person you trust with private thoughts and secrets. (Often spelled 'confidante' for a woman.)
examples: She has been my confidante since primary school.

cards.meaning: Firm, loyal and unwavering.
examples: He remained a steadfast friend through difficult times.

cards.meaning: To like each other immediately.
examples: We hit it off on the first day of orientation.

cards.meaning: A friend who is only there when things are going well.
examples: When I lost my job, I learned who my fair-weather friends were.

cards.meaning: Mutual trust and friendship among people who spend a lot of time together.
examples: There was a strong camaraderie among the volunteers.

cards.meaning: To gradually become less close.
examples: We drifted apart after university.

cards.meaning: To support someone, especially in a difficult situation.
examples: Her friends stood by her throughout the crisis.

cards.meaning: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other well.
examples: A good lecturer builds rapport with students.

cards.meaning: Someone who listens and comforts you when you are upset.
examples: He was always there as a shoulder to cry on.

cards.meaning: To have known each other for a long time.
examples: Mei and I go back a long way.

title: Decision Making
description: Words for weighing options, hesitating and finally choosing.

cards.meaning: To think about something carefully and slowly before deciding.
examples: We deliberated for an hour before choosing the venue.

cards.meaning: Uncertain and slow to act or decide, showing doubt.
examples: She was hesitant about accepting the offer without more details.

cards.meaning: Able to make choices quickly and confidently.
examples: A good manager is decisive when the team is unsure.

cards.meaning: To consider the advantages and disadvantages of something before deciding.
examples: I need to weigh up the costs before committing to the trip.

cards.meaning: To doubt or criticise a decision after it has been made, often your own.
examples: Stop second-guessing yourself — the choice was sound.

cards.meaning: Unable to decide between two choices, feeling pulled in both directions.
examples: I'm torn between the job in KL and staying near my family.

cards.meaning: To choose one thing from a set of possibilities.
examples: We opted for the earlier flight to avoid the rush.

cards.meaning: Firmly determined to do something, unlikely to be persuaded otherwise.
examples: She was resolute about finishing the degree in two years.

cards.meaning: Undecided between two options, avoiding commitment to either.
examples: Two committee members are still on the fence about the merger.

cards.meaning: Affecting many things at once; wide in range (often of decisions or changes).
examples: The new CEO announced sweeping changes to the whole company.

title: Ambition and Drive
description: Words for wanting more, working hard and chasing goals.

cards.meaning: Hoping to become a particular kind of professional or achieve a role.
examples: She is an aspiring novelist who writes before work each morning.

cards.meaning: Strongly motivated to succeed, with energy that pushes through obstacles.
examples: He is driven by a desire to prove the critics wrong.

cards.meaning: To make a great effort to achieve something difficult.
examples: We strive to answer every email within a day.

cards.meaning: Never stopping or giving up, sometimes to an intense degree.
examples: Her relentless practice turned a weakness into a strength.

cards.meaning: A strong hope or ambition for the future, often a career or life goal.
examples: His aspiration is to run his own clinic by forty.

cards.meaning: To advance step by step to higher positions in a career.
examples: She climbed the ladder from intern to regional director in eight years.

cards.meaning: The quality of holding on firmly to a goal and refusing to give up.
examples: His tenacity impressed the scouts more than his talent.

cards.meaning: An energetic, determined person who actively makes things happen.
examples: The startup was built by three go-getters still in university.

cards.meaning: An extremely strong want that motivates constant action.
examples: A burning desire to travel shaped every choice she made.

cards.meaning: To try to achieve more than is realistic or safe.
examples: The firm overreached by opening three branches in one year.

title: Failure and Resilience
description: Words for falling short, recovering and trying again.

cards.meaning: A problem that delays or reverses progress, usually temporary.
examples: The funding cut was a setback, but the project survived.

cards.meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulties and carry on.
examples: Children are often more resilient than adults expect.

cards.meaning: A complete failure, especially of a product, show or event.
examples: The film was a flop at the box office but became a cult classic.

cards.meaning: To recover well after a disappointment or failure.
examples: He bounced back from the injury within a season.

cards.meaning: To make a mistake or lose progress briefly, without falling completely.
examples: She stumbled in the second round but won the third.

cards.meaning: Serious difficulty or misfortune over a period of time.
examples: The team showed real character in adversity.

cards.meaning: To learn something through painful experience rather than advice.
examples: I learned the hard way that backups matter.

cards.meaning: To recover your confidence and energy after a fall or failure.
cards.examples: After the bankruptcy she picked herself up and started again.

cards.meaning: Not troubled or shaken by something difficult or surprising.
examples: He seemed completely unfazed by the criticism.

cards.meaning: To become better or stronger because of a hard experience.
examples: She says she grew more from the failures than the wins.

title: Weather and Atmosphere
description: Words that describe skies, moods in the air and the feel of a moment.

cards.meaning: Cloudy and grey, with the sun completely hidden.
examples: The sky stayed overcast all afternoon.

cards.meaning: Light rain in very fine drops, slower than proper rain.
examples: A thin drizzle settled over the city by evening.

cards.meaning: Describing air that feels heavy and damp with moisture.
examples: The morning was so humid that the windows fogged over.

cards.meaning: Dark and depressing, of weather or of mood and places.
examples: The waiting room felt gloomy in the fading light.

cards.meaning: Pleasantly dry, cold and fresh, typically of autumn air.
examples: We walked out into the crisp air of the highlands.

cards.meaning: Extremely hot and uncomfortable, in a way that exhausts.
examples: The stadium was sweltering at midday.

cards.meaning: A thin layer of tiny water drops close to the ground, softer than fog.
examples: Mist hung over the paddy fields at dawn.

cards.meaning: A sudden heavy fall of rain.
examples: We sheltered from the downpour under the petrol station roof.

cards.meaning: Warm and pleasant, in a gentle, soothing way.
examples: A balmy breeze came off the sea after dinner.

cards.meaning: Cold, empty and cheerless, of landscapes or prospects.
examples: The coastline looked bleak under the grey clouds.

title: Etiquette and Manners
description: Words for polite behaviour, social rules and graceful conduct.

cards.meaning: Polite and respectful towards others, especially in formal settings.
examples: The staff were courteous even at the end of a long shift.

cards.meaning: Careful not to offend, saying difficult things in a kind way.
examples: Her tactful reply saved the meeting.

cards.meaning: Careful to keep things private and avoid attracting attention.
examples: He was discreet about the salary discussion.

cards.meaning: Polite behaviour or a small act of respect.
examples: Returning the call within a day is a basic courtesy.

cards.meaning: An embarrassing social mistake, usually of etiquette or custom.
examples: Asking her age at the dinner was a real faux pas.

cards.meaning: Kind, polite and generous, especially to those below one in status.
examples: The host was gracious to every guest, however late they arrived.

cards.meaning: The accepted rules of behaviour in formal or official situations.
examples: Seating protocol at state dinners is planned in detail.

cards.meaning: Light, polite conversation about unimportant things, to be social.
examples: He mastered the art of small talk in elevators.

cards.meaning: Basic polite behaviour expected of everyone, nothing special.
examples: Replying to invitations is common courtesy, not a favour.

cards.meaning: To refuse an offer in a soft, respectful manner.
examples: I politely declined the second helping.

title: Learning and Study
description: Words for absorbing knowledge, practising and mastering skills.

cards.meaning: To understand something fully and confidently.
examples: She grasped the concept after the second example.

cards.meaning: To keep knowledge in your memory over time.
examples: Taking notes by hand helps me retain the material.

cards.meaning: To study intensively in a short time, usually before an exam.
examples: He crammed the entire syllabus the night before.

cards.meaning: Mechanical repetition from memory without understanding.
examples: Reciting formulas by rote won't help you apply them.

cards.meaning: To make an idea or skill part of how you naturally think and act.
examples: After a year, the safety habits were internalised.

cards.meaning: A process where a lot must be learned very quickly at the start.
examples: The new role had a steep learning curve, but he enjoyed it.

cards.meaning: The regular routines and methods a person uses to study.
examples: Good study habits matter more than long hours.

cards.meaning: To quickly improve or refresh knowledge you once had.
examples: I need to brush up on my Japanese before the trip.

cards.meaning: To learn something casually, without formal teaching.
examples: She picked up most of her English from games and films.

cards.meaning: Able to express ideas clearly in words; or to express something clearly.
examples: He is remarkably articulate for a nine-year-old.

title: Apologies and Forgiveness
description: Words for admitting wrong, making peace and moving on.

cards.meaning: To express regret for something you did wrong.
examples: He apologised for arriving late to the interview.

cards.meaning: A feeling of sadness about something you did or failed to do.
examples: Her only regret was not starting sooner.

cards.meaning: To do something good to balance a wrong you caused.
examples: He tried to make amends by fixing the damage himself.

cards.meaning: To admit responsibility for something, often reluctantly.
examples: Someone owned up to breaking the window before the teacher asked.

cards.meaning: To stop being angry or holding a grudge about something.
examples: They argued for years before finally letting it go.

cards.meaning: To keep bad feelings towards someone long after the event.
examples: He never bore a grudge, even against his rivals.

cards.meaning: To restore a friendly relationship after a conflict.
examples: The brothers reconciled at the wedding after a decade.

cards.meaning: Genuine and honest, without pretence or hidden motive.
examples: Her apology sounded sincere, so I accepted it.

cards.meaning: Resentment or anger remaining after a disagreement.
examples: No hard feelings — it was a fair competition.

cards.meaning: To discuss a problem openly to remove tension and misunderstanding.
examples: We finally cleared the air over coffee yesterday.

title: Money and Budgets
description: Everyday words for spending, saving and the cost of living.

cards.meaning: A plan for how money will be spent, or to plan spending limits.
examples: We budgeted RM50 a week for food.

cards.meaning: Money that must be spent, especially regularly for living or working.
examples: Travel expenses are covered by the company.

cards.meaning: Careful with money, avoiding waste, without being stingy.
examples: Her frugal habits let her retire at fifty.

cards.meaning: To spend a lot on something unnecessary but enjoyable, occasionally.
examples: We splurged on a weekend at the hot springs.

cards.meaning: To keep money aside over time for a particular goal.
examples: They saved up for two years before the renovation.

cards.meaning: To spend less than you earn, avoiding debt.
examples: Living within your means is harder than it sounds in the city.

cards.meaning: To be extremely careful with small amounts of money.
examples: We pinched pennies through our student years.

cards.meaning: Money left after taxes and necessities, free to spend or save.
examples: Their disposable income shrank after the rent increase.

cards.meaning: The general level of prices for everyday needs in a place.
examples: The cost of living in KL keeps climbing.

cards.meaning: To put money into something expecting benefit later; also used non-financially.
examples: Invest in a good chair if you work from home.

title: Describing People
description: Precise words for character and personality, beyond 'nice' and 'kind'.

cards.meaning: Careful not to inconvenience others; thinking of their comfort.
examples: A considerate neighbour kept the music down after ten.

cards.meaning: Refusing to change an opinion or course of action, even when wrong.
examples: He was too stubborn to ask for directions.

cards.meaning: Relaxed and tolerant, not easily worried or offended.
examples: Her easygoing manner made the trip stress-free.

cards.meaning: Extremely careful about small details, precise in everything.
examples: His meticulous notes saved us during the audit.

cards.meaning: Saying exactly what you think, even when it is unpopular.
examples: The outspoken critic refused to soften her reviews.

cards.meaning: Sensible and humble despite success or attention.
examples: Fame never changed her; she stayed grounded.

cards.meaning: Too ready to believe things, and therefore easy to trick.
examples: The scam targets gullible buyers of cheap tickets.

cards.meaning: Having a natural charm that draws and inspires other people.
examples: The charismatic coach turned a weak team into believers.

cards.meaning: Quiet and keeping feelings private, slow to open up.
examples: He is reserved at first, but loyal once you know him.

cards.meaning: Confident in yourself and your abilities, without arrogance.
examples: She walked into the interview calm and self-assured.

title: Change and Transition
description: Words for times of life change, adjustment and new beginnings.

cards.meaning: The process of changing from one state or stage to another.
examples: The transition to the new system took three months.

cards.meaning: To change something slightly to fit a new situation, or adapt yourself.
examples: It took a term to adjust to the new schedule.

cards.meaning: The moment when an important change of direction happens.
examples: The scholarship was a turning point in her life.

cards.meaning: To become comfortable in a new place, job or routine.
examples: The new students settled in by the second week.

cards.meaning: A new beginning, leaving past problems behind.
examples: The move to Penang gave them a fresh start.

cards.meaning: A big, disruptive change that disturbs normal life.
examples: The merger caused a year of upheaval.

cards.meaning: To change your behaviour or habits to suit new conditions.
examples: Retailers adapted quickly to online orders.

cards.meaning: To accept and welcome change rather than resist it.
examples: The team embraced change instead of fearing it.

cards.meaning: A period in life or history, viewed as one part of a longer story.
examples: Closing the shop ended a chapter of forty years.

cards.meaning: In a situation that is unfamiliar and challenging for you.
examples: Teaching pushed her far out of her comfort zone.

title: Opinions and Debate
description: Words for stating views, agreeing, disagreeing and persuading.

cards.meaning: A particular way of seeing or judging a matter.
examples: From a student's point of view, the policy is unfair.

cards.meaning: To admit that something is true after first disagreeing.
examples: I concede that my first plan was too expensive.

cards.meaning: So convincing or strong that it forces attention or agreement.
examples: She made a compelling case for the four-day week.

cards.meaning: To argue against a claim, showing why it is wrong.
examples: He rebutted each objection with data.

cards.meaning: Unfairly favouring one side, judged by preference rather than fact.
examples: The coverage was biased towards the home team.

cards.meaning: To argue the opposite side to test an idea, not from real belief.
examples: Let me play devil's advocate: what if demand falls?

cards.meaning: Points that both sides agree on, despite other differences.
examples: They found common ground on funding, if not timing.

cards.meaning: To decide something is true too quickly, without enough evidence.
examples: Don't jump to conclusions until the report is out.

cards.meaning: Based on clear, logical thinking; carefully argued.
examples: It was a well-reasoned essay with strong evidence.

cards.meaning: To end an argument by accepting that neither side will change.
examples: We agreed to disagree about the ending.

title: Work and Careers
description: Words for jobs, workplace life and professional growth.

cards.meaning: The latest time by which work must be finished.
examples: The deadline for applications is Friday noon.

cards.meaning: A person you work with, especially in a professional job.
examples: My colleagues covered my tasks during the hospital stay.

cards.meaning: A move to a higher, more senior position at work.
examples: She earned the promotion after the launch.

cards.meaning: To give tasks to other people, usually those you manage.
examples: Good leaders delegate tasks they cannot do themselves.

cards.meaning: Exhaustion from long stress that kills motivation and energy.
examples: He took a month off to recover from burnout.

cards.meaning: To accept new work or responsibility.
examples: Don't take on more than you can finish well.

cards.meaning: Involving direct, practical involvement rather than just theory.
examples: The course is hands-on: you build a real project.

cards.meaning: (Of a career) to rise gradually in position or salary over time.
examples: He climbed from intern to director in nine years.

cards.meaning: To build professional relationships; the set of contacts itself.
examples: She networked at every conference, and it paid off.

cards.meaning: The amount of work a person has to handle in a period.
examples: Our workload doubles every exam season.

title: Communication Styles
description: Words for how people speak, write and get their meaning across.

cards.meaning: Saying things directly, with little softening — honest but sometimes rude.
examples: His blunt feedback upset the intern.

cards.meaning: To express an idea clearly in words.
examples: She articulated the vision in two sentences.

cards.meaning: Using far more words than needed; wordy.
examples: The report was so verbose that nobody finished it.

cards.meaning: Brief and clear, expressing the idea in the fewest necessary words.
examples: Keep the summary succinct: one page.

cards.meaning: To say the main matter immediately, without introduction.
examples: I'll get straight to the point: we missed the target.

cards.meaning: To avoid the main subject, talking around it instead of facing it.
examples: Stop beating around the bush and name the problem.

cards.meaning: To speak at length, wandering from point to point without focus.
examples: He rambled for ten minutes before reaching the question.

cards.meaning: Fluent and persuasive in speech or writing, moving listeners.
examples: Her eloquent speech brought the hall to its feet.

cards.meaning: A failure to share meaning correctly, causing misunderstanding.
examples: The delay was pure miscommunication about the time zone.

cards.meaning: To express something in an understated, gentle way, implying more.
examples: He was annoyed, to put it mildly.

title: Risk and Caution
description: Words for taking chances, playing safe and facing uncertainty.

cards.meaning: A risky action with an uncertain outcome, taken hoping for gain.
examples: Quitting without a plan was a gamble — it worked.

cards.meaning: Careful to avoid danger or mistakes; unhurried in decisions.
examples: Be cautious about offers that sound too good.

cards.meaning: To choose the least risky option available.
examples: We played it safe and launched with the tested version.

cards.meaning: A risk taken deliberately, after weighing the odds.
examples: Moving abroad alone was a calculated risk.

cards.meaning: At risk of being lost or won, in a given situation.
examples: Jobs are at stake if the factory closes.

cards.meaning: Acting without care for danger or consequences.
examples: Reckless overtaking caused the crash.

cards.meaning: To reduce risk by supporting more than one option.
examples: Apply to both universities — hedge your bets.

cards.meaning: A decision to trust something without proof, despite uncertainty.
examples: Joining the startup felt like a leap of faith.

cards.meaning: A hidden danger or difficulty that traps the unwary.
examples: The guide lists the common pitfalls for new freelancers.

cards.meaning: A choice almost certain to succeed, though not exciting.
examples: Studying early is always a safe bet before exams.

title: Success and Achievement
description: Words for winning, reaching goals and celebrating milestones.

cards.meaning: To succeed in doing or finishing something, especially something hard.
examples: She accomplished more in a year than most do in five.

cards.meaning: An important event marking progress in a long journey.
examples: The first paying customer was a real milestone.

cards.meaning: A major achievement or decision that changes everything after it.
examples: The ruling was a landmark for workers' rights.

cards.meaning: A sudden, important discovery or advance after a long struggle.
examples: The team's breakthrough came after midnight, typically.

cards.meaning: To do better than someone else, or better than before.
examples: This year's sales outdid every forecast.

cards.meaning: (Of effort) to bring good results after a period of waiting.
examples: Ten years of practice finally paid off at the finals.

cards.meaning: Succeeding although the chances were strongly unfavourable.
examples: They won the championship against all the odds.

cards.meaning: An achievement worth being proud of; an honour.
examples: Publishing at nineteen was quite a feather in her cap.

cards.meaning: A great victory or success, after difficulty.
examples: Finishing the thesis felt like a quiet triumph.

cards.meaning: Fully earned through effort, worth every bit of praise.
examples: Enjoy the holiday — it's well-deserved.
